name: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-17
lead: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-17 is a cosmetic signal peptide, a short chain of five amino acids joined to a fatty acid so that it can sit in a serum and be applied to the skin. It is associated with lash and brow serums and with skin-care products that aim at a smoother, fuller look. The lash-and-brow ingredient sold by suppliers is usually listed under the INCI name Myristoyl Pentapeptide-17, a closely named variant that carries a myristic rather than palmitic fatty-acid tail, and the two names are often used interchangeably in discussion.[1]

Suppliers describe the peptide as supporting keratin production and follicle activity in order to make lashes and brows look longer and denser, and as a component of lash serums, brow enhancers, conditioners and treatment mascaras.[1] The supplier page cited here does not publish clinical data; no published human trial of the ingredient was found.

chain: Peptide applied to the lash line or brow in a serum
Marketed to support keratin synthesis and follicle activity
Longer, fuller-looking lashes and brows over weeks of use
angle.text: People use serums containing this peptide on the lash line or brows hoping for longer, thicker-looking lashes and brows. Suppliers say it works by supporting keratin production and follicle activity, and it is also included in some anti-aging formulas.

infobox: Lash serums, brow serums, lash conditioners[1]

paras: The peptide is listed by suppliers for eyelash serums, lash conditioners and primers, eyebrow growth serums and mascaras with treatment claims.[1] It is also mentioned among general anti-aging signal peptides.

The supplier states that the peptide enhances lash and brow growth by stimulating keratin synthesis and supporting follicle activity, and lists follicle markers including VEGF, beta-catenin, bFGF and collagen III as being upregulated, along with reduced lash fallout.[1] These statements are made by the supplier.
No studies found. Supplier material cites laboratory (in vitro) work on keratin gene expression rather than published human trials.[1]

Cosmetic peptides are applied topically at low concentrations; suppliers give use levels in the range of hundredths of a percent. Eye-area products are generally advised to be patch-tested, and product labels give guidance on irritation.

card.summary: A cosmetic peptide in lash and brow serums, marketed to support keratin and follicle activity for longer, fuller-looking lashes and brows.
card.note: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; supplier claims are not backed by published human trials.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl pentapeptide-17 is a short cosmetic peptide used in lash and brow serums. The lash-grade ingredient is usually listed as myristoyl pentapeptide-17.

People apply it along the lash line or brows hoping for longer, thicker-looking lashes and brows, and it also appears in some anti-aging products.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers say it supports keratin synthesis and hair-follicle activity. These statements come from suppliers and are based on laboratory work.
quick.risks: It is a topical cosmetic ingredient used at very low concentrations. As with any eye-area product, irritation is the main practical concern.
